summary: Explains how RTP sessions are synchronised and how quickly this can happen. It shows that most sessions synchronise immediately, but video switching conference units or large source-specific multicast groups can add delay, which can be unacceptable for some uses.

plainLanguage.summary: When you watch a video call, the picture and the sound have to be played at the same moment. This RFC explains how the timing information that makes that possible is carried, how long a receiver waits before it can start, and three changes that make the wait shorter.

questions: how to synchronise audio and video in rtp
what are the ntp rtp header extensions
subtitle: How RTP streams are lined up in time, how long that takes, and three ways to make it faster.

tldr.problem: A video call carries audio and video in separate RTP streams with separate media clocks, and a receiver cannot play them together until it has enough timing information from each stream.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC measures the delay this causes, then defines three backwards compatible extensions: an immediate first report for source-specific multicast senders, a new feedback message that asks for an extra sender report, and two RTP header extensions that carry the time reference inside the data packets.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from November 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3550 and registers one new feedback format and two new RTP header extension URIs.

facts.label: RTCP-SR-REQ feedback format
facts.value: FMT 5, an empty Feedback Control Information, and a length of 2

facts.label: RTCP share of session bandwidth
facts.value: Generally 5%, split one quarter to senders and three quarters to receivers

facts.label: Minimum reporting interval
facts.value: 5 seconds, or 360 divided by the bandwidth in kbit/s above 72 kbit/s

facts.label: Report timing randomisation
facts.value: Between 0.5 and 1.5 times the reporting interval

today: RFC 6051 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3550 with the new feedback message and header extensions, and it notes that the extensions are not specific to layered coding and can be used in any environment where synchronisation latency matters.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When RTP delivers multimedia content it is often necessary to synchronise the playout of the audio and video components of a presentation. This is achieved using information contained in the RTP Control Protocol sender report packets of RFC 3550. Those packets are sent periodically, and the components of a multimedia session cannot be synchronised until sufficient sender reports have been received for each RTP flow, to allow the receiver to establish mappings between the media clock used for each flow and the common NTP-format reference clock used to establish synchronisation.

Concern has been expressed that this synchronisation delay is problematic for some applications, for example those using layered or multi-description video coding. This memo reviews the operations of RTP synchronisation, describes the synchronisation delay that can be expected, and proposes three backwards compatible extensions to the basic RTP synchronisation mechanism.

  • The RTCP transmission timing rules are relaxed for source-specific multicast senders, to reduce the initial synchronisation latency for large SSM groups.
  • An enhancement to the extended RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback, RTP/AVPF from RFC 4585, allows receivers to request additional RTCP sender report packets, providing the metadata needed to synchronise RTP flows. This can reduce the synchronisation delay when joining sessions with large RTCP reporting intervals, in the presence of packet loss, or when video switching multiplexers are employed.
  • Two RTP header extensions are defined, to deliver synchronisation metadata in band with RTP data packets. These extensions provide synchronisation metadata that is aligned with RTP data packets, and so eliminate the need to estimate clock skew between flows before synchronisation. They can also reduce the need to receive RTCP sender reports before flows can be synchronised, although they do not eliminate the need for RTCP.

The immediate use case for these extensions is to reduce the delay due to synchronisation when joining a layered video session, for example an H.264 SVC session in Non-Interleaved Timestamp-based mode. The extensions are not specific to layered coding, however, and can be used in any environment when synchronisation latency is an issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Each media stream has its own clock, so the receiver has to be told how each clock lines up with real time before it can play them together. That information normally arrives in a separate report packet, which is only sent every few seconds, and this RFC looks at ways to get it sooner.

sections.title: How RTP Flows Are Synchronised
sections.content:
RTP flows are synchronised by receivers based on information contained in the RTCP sender report packets generated by senders, specifically the NTP-format timestamp and the RTP timestamp. Synchronisation requires that a common reference clock must be used to generate the NTP-format timestamps in a set of flows that are to be synchronised. When synchronising several RTP flows, the RTP timestamps for each flow are derived from separate, media specific clocks, but the NTP-format timestamps in the sender reports of all flows to be synchronised must be sampled from the same clock. To achieve faster and more accurate synchronisation it is further recommended that senders and receivers use a synchronised common NTP-format reference clock with common properties, especially timebase, where possible. The means by which that common reference clock and its properties are signalled and distributed is outside the scope of the memo.

Each type of media, such as audio or video, is sent in a separate RTP session, and the receiver associates the RTP flows to be synchronised by means of the canonical end-point identifier, or CNAME, item included in the RTCP Source Description packets generated by the sender or signalled out of band. For layered media, different layers can be sent in different RTP sessions, or using different synchronisation source values within a single RTP session; in both cases the CNAME is used to identify the flows to be synchronised. To ensure synchronisation, an RTP sender must therefore send periodic compound RTCP packets following Section 6 of RFC 3550.

The timing of those packets depends on the number of members in each RTP session, the fraction of them that are sending data, the session bandwidth, the configured RTCP bandwidth fraction, and whether the session is multicast or unicast. In summary, RTCP control traffic is allocated a small fraction, generally 5%, of the session bandwidth. Of that fraction, one quarter is allocated to active RTP senders, while receivers use the remaining three quarters, and these fractions can be configured through the Session Description Protocol. Each member derives an RTCP reporting interval based on those fractions, whether the session is multicast or unicast, the number of members it has observed, and whether it is actively sending data.

Each member then sends a compound RTCP packet on average once per reporting interval, with the actual transmission time randomised in the range 0.5 to 1.5 times the reporting interval to avoid synchronisation of reports. A minimum reporting interval of 5 seconds is recommended, except that the delay before sending the initial report may be set to half the minimum interval to allow quicker notification that the new participant is present. For unicast sessions the delay before sending the initial compound RTCP packet may be zero. In addition, for unicast sessions and for active senders in a multicast session, the fixed minimum reporting interval may be scaled to 360 divided by the session bandwidth in kilobits per second, which is smaller than 5 seconds for bandwidths greater than 72 kilobits per second.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender reports its own clock against the shared network time clock, and the receiver lines the two up. Reports are sent on a timer that grows with the size of the group, so a big session reports less often. The timing of each report is deliberately jittered so that many reports do not arrive together.

sections.title: Initial Synchronisation Delay
sections.content:
A multimedia session comprises a set of concurrent RTP sessions among a common group of participants, using one RTP session for each media type. A videoconference, for instance, might contain an audio RTP session and a video RTP session. To allow a receiver to synchronise the components of a multimedia session, a compound RTCP packet containing a sender report and a Source Description packet with a CNAME item must be sent to each of the RTP sessions in the multimedia session by each sender. A receiver cannot synchronise playout across the session until such packets have been received on all of the component RTP sessions. If there is no packet loss, this gives an expected initial synchronisation delay equal to the average time taken to receive the first RTCP packet in the RTP session with the longest RTCP reporting interval. The initial synchronisation delay for layered sessions is similar, since the layers cannot be synchronised until the sender report and CNAME information has been received for each layer.

Unicast sessions. For unicast multimedia or layered sessions, senders should transmit an initial compound RTCP packet immediately on joining each RTP session. The individual RTP sessions are considered joined once any in-band signalling for NAT traversal and any security keying has concluded and the media path is open. This implies the initial RTCP packet is sent in parallel with the first data packet, and in the absence of packet loss, flows can be synchronised immediately. It is expected that NAT pinholes, firewall holes, quality of service, and media security keys will have been negotiated as part of the signalling before the first RTCP packet is sent, which should ensure that middleboxes are ready to accept traffic and reduce the likelihood that the initial RTCP packet is lost.

Source-specific multicast sessions. For multicast sessions, the delay before sending the initial RTCP packet, and hence the synchronisation delay, varies with the session bandwidth and the number of members in the session. The average synchronisation delay depends on the slowest of the component RTP sessions, which will generally be the session with the lowest bandwidth, assuming all the RTP sessions have the same number of members. The reduced minimum RTCP reporting interval of 360 seconds divided by the session bandwidth in kilobits per second should be used when synchronisation latency is likely to be an issue, and the reporting interval is halved for the first RTCP packet.

The table below reproduces the RFC's Figure 1, the average initial synchronisation delay in seconds for an RTP session with one sender. These numbers assume a source-specific multicast channel with a single active sender and an average RTCP packet size of 70 octets. These intervals are sufficient for lip-synchronisation without excessive delay, but might be viewed as having too much latency for synchronising parts of a layered video stream. The RTCP interval is randomised in the usual manner, so the minimum synchronisation delay is half these intervals and the maximum is 1.5 times them. The intervals are also calculated assuming perfect knowledge of the number of members in the session.

Any-source multicast sessions. For ASM sessions, the fraction of members that are senders plays an important role and causes more variation in the average RTCP reporting interval. The initial synchronisation delay scales with the number of senders, so that the total RTCP traffic from all group members does not grow without bound, and it can be significantly larger than for source-specific groups. Despite this, the initial synchronisation time remains acceptable for lip-synchronisation in typical small to medium sized group video conferencing scenarios. Multi-sender groups implemented with multi-unicast through a central RTP translator or mixer, or some forms of video switching multiplexer, distribute RTCP packets to all members of the group and so scale in the same way.

Discussion. For unicast sessions the existing sender report mechanism allows immediate synchronisation, provided the initial RTCP packet is not lost. For SSM sessions the delay is sufficient for lip-synchronisation but may be larger than desired for some layered codecs. The reason immediate RTCP packets are not sent for multicast groups is to avoid an implosion of requests when large numbers of members join the group at once, the so-called flash crowd. That is not an issue for SSM senders, since there can be at most one sender, so it is desirable to allow SSM senders to send an immediate sender report on joining a session. Receivers in an SSM session that send unicast feedback are not allowed to send immediate RTCP. For ASM sessions, implosion of responses is a concern, so no change is proposed to the RTCP timing rules.

In all cases it is possible that the initial sender report packet is lost. The receiver then cannot synchronise the media until the reporting interval has passed and the next sender report is sent, which is undesirable.
sections.plainLanguage: With a small unicast session the wait is normally nothing. With a large multicast group it can be several seconds, and the more senders in the group the longer it gets, because the reporting interval has to stretch to keep the total control traffic bounded.

sections.title: Sources of Delay and the Three Extensions
sections.content:
Synchronisation between RTP sessions is potentially slower for late joiners than for participants present at the start of a session, for three reasons.

First, many of the optimisations that allow rapid transmission of sender reports apply only at the start of a session. A new participant may have to wait a complete RTCP reporting interval for each session before receiving the data it needs to synchronise the media streams, which might take several seconds depending on the configured session bandwidth and the number of participants.

Second, the nature of the RTCP timing rules adds delay. Packets are generated on average once per reporting interval, but the exact transmission times are randomised by plus or minus 50% to avoid synchronisation of reports. That avoids network congestion in multicast sessions, but it also means the timing of the sender reports for different RTP sessions is not synchronised. A receiver must therefore estimate the skew on the NTP-format clock in order to align RTP timestamps across sessions. That estimation is an essential part of an RTP synchronisation implementation and can be done with high accuracy given sufficient reports, but collecting sufficient sender report data to perform it may require reception of several reports, further increasing the delay.

Third, many media codecs have the notion of periodic access points, so that a newly joined receiver often cannot start decoding a media stream until the packets corresponding to the access point have been received. These access points may be sent less often than sender reports, and so may be the limiting factor in starting synchronised media playout for late joiners. The RTP extension for unicast-based rapid acquisition of multicast RTP sessions may be used to reduce the time taken to receive the access points in some scenarios.

These delays are likely an issue when tuning in to an ongoing multicast RTP session, or for video switching multiplexers.

Three backwards compatible RTP extensions are defined to reduce the possible synchronisation delay: a reduced initial RTCP interval for SSM senders, a rapid resynchronisation request message, and RTP header extensions that can convey synchronisation metadata in band.

Reduced initial RTCP interval for SSM senders. In SSM sessions where the initial synchronisation delay is important, the RTP sender may set the delay before sending the initial compound RTCP packet to zero, and send its first RTCP packet immediately upon joining the SSM session. This is purely a local change to the sender, implementable as a configurable option. RTP receivers in an SSM session that send unicast RTCP feedback must not send RTCP packets with zero initial delay, and the timing rules of RFC 5760 apply unchanged to them.

Rapid resynchronisation request. A receiver that cannot synchronise because a sender report was lost can send a new feedback message asking the media source to produce a sender report as soon as possible, within the constraints of the RTCP timing rules for early feedback. A media source that understands it should generate a sender report as soon as possible while complying with the RTCP early feedback rules. If the use of non-compound RTCP was previously negotiated, both the feedback request and the sender report response may be sent as non-compound RTCP packets. The request may be repeated once per RTCP reporting interval if no sender report is forthcoming. The media source may ignore the request if its regular schedule can be expected to let the receiver synchronise within a reasonable time frame. In SSM sessions with unicast feedback, the feedback target and the media source may not be co-located, in which case the request should be forwarded to the media source, although the forwarding mechanism is not defined here. If the feedback target provides a network management interface, it might be useful to log which receivers send the request and which do not, since the ones that do not will see slower stream synchronisation.

In-band delivery of synchronisation metadata. The RTP header extension mechanism of RFC 5285 can be adapted to carry an optional NTP-format timestamp in RTP data packets, aligned with the data rather than with the control channel. These extensions also reduce the need to receive sender reports before flows can be synchronised, although they do not eliminate the need for RTCP.
sections.plainLanguage:
Joining late is harder for three reasons. The fast first report only happens at the start. Reports are sent at jittered times, so the receiver has to work out how far the clocks drift apart. And the codec may not send anything decodable until the next key frame, which can be further away than the next report.

Three changes, all optional and all backwards compatible: let a single-source multicast sender speak immediately when it joins, let a receiver ask for an extra report when it is stuck, and put the time reference inside the data packets themselves.

sections.title: The Rapid Resynchronisation Request
sections.content:
The general format of an RTP/AVPF transport layer feedback message is a two-bit version field set to 2, a padding bit, a five-bit FMT field, an eight-bit payload type of RTPFB which is 205, a 16-bit length field, the 32-bit SSRC of the packet sender, the 32-bit SSRC of the media source, and the Feedback Control Information.

One new feedback message type is defined, RTCP-SR-REQ, with FMT set to 5. The Feedback Control Information part of the feedback message must be empty. The SSRC of the packet sender indicates the member that is unable to synchronise media streams, while the SSRC of the media source indicates the sender of the media it is unable to synchronise. The length must equal 2.

If the RTP/AVPF profile is in use, this feedback message may be sent by a receiver to indicate that it is unable to synchronise some media streams and desires that the media source transmit an RTCP sender report as soon as possible, within the constraints of the RTCP timing rules for early feedback. When it receives such an indication, a media source that understands the RTCP-SR-REQ packet should generate a sender report as soon as possible while complying with the RTCP early feedback rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a small feedback packet with a format number of 5. It carries two identifiers and no other data: who is stuck, and whose stream they are waiting for.

sections.title: In-Band Synchronisation Metadata
sections.content:
The RTP header extension mechanism defined in RFC 5285 can be adapted to carry an optional NTP-format timestamp in RTP data packets. If such a timestamp is included, it must correspond to the same time instant as the RTP timestamp in the packet's header, and must be derived from the same clock used to generate the NTP-format timestamps included in RTCP sender reports. Provided it has knowledge of the SSRC to CNAME mapping, either from prior receipt of an RTCP CNAME packet or via out-of-band signalling, the receiver can use the information as input to the synchronisation algorithm, in exactly the same way as if an additional sender report had been received for the flow.

Two variants are defined. Variant A extends the RTP header with a 64-bit NTP-format timestamp as defined in RFC 5905. Variant B carries the lower 24-bit part of the Seconds of an NTP-format timestamp and the 32 bits of the Fraction of an NTP-format timestamp.

An NTP-format timestamp may be included in any RTP packets the sender chooses, but it is recommended when performing timestamp-based decoding order recovery for layered codecs carried in multiple RTP flows. The header extension should also be sent in the RTP packets corresponding to a video random access point, and in the associated audio packets, to allow rapid synchronisation for late joiners in multimedia sessions, and in video switching scenarios.

The RFC notes two drawbacks. Including an RTP header extension reduces the efficiency of RTP header compression if it is used, and middleboxes that do not understand the header extensions may remove them or may not update the content according to this memo.

In all cases, irrespective of whether in-band NTP-format timestamps are included, regular RTCP sender report packets must be sent, to provide backwards compatibility with receivers that synchronise RTP flows according to RFC 3550 and robustness in the face of middleboxes that might strip RTP header extensions. If the Variant B 56-bit extension is used, RTCP sender reports must be used to derive the upper 8 bits of the Seconds of the NTP-format timestamp.

When SDP is used, the use of the RTP header extensions must be indicated as specified in RFC 5285, using the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ntp-64 for Variant A and the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ntp-56 for Variant B.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of waiting for a separate report, the sender can stamp each data packet with the time it represents. The receiver then knows the alignment without having to work it out from scattered reports. The shorter variant leaves out some bits, which have to be filled in from a report instead.

sections.title: Decoding Order Recovery in Layered Codecs
sections.content:
Packets in RTP flows are often predictively coded, with a receiver having to arrange the packets into a particular order before it can decode the media data. The decoding order might be specified explicitly as a field in the RTP payload header, or the receiver might decode the packets in order of their RTP timestamps. If a layered encoding is used, where the media data is split across several RTP flows, it is often necessary to exactly synchronise the RTP flows comprising the different layers before layers other than the base layer can be decoded. Examples are H.264 SVC in Non-Interleaved Timestamp-based mode and MPEG surround multi-channel audio.

In-band synchronisation. When a layered, multi-description or multi-view codec is used, with the different components of the media transferred on separate RTP flows, the RTP sender should use periodic synchronous in-band delivery of synchronisation metadata. There are three parts to this. The sender must negotiate the use of the header extensions and must periodically and synchronously insert them into all the RTP flows forming the separate components of the flow. Synchronous insertion requires the sender to insert the header extensions into packets corresponding to exactly the same sampling instant in all the flows, so that the extensions have identical NTP-format timestamps and receivers can exactly align the RTP timestamps for the component flows. That may require inserting extra data packets into some component flows, if some flows contain packets for sampling instants that do not exist in other flows, for example a layered video codec where the layers have differing frame rates. The frequency of insertion corresponds directly to the synchronisation latency: more frequent insertion means higher per-flow overheads but lower synchronisation latency. It is recommended that the sender insert the header extensions synchronously into all component RTP flows at least once per random access point of the media, though they may be inserted more often.

The sender must continue to send periodic RTCP reports including sender reports, and must ensure the RTP timestamp to NTP-format timestamp mapping in those reports is consistent with the mapping used in the header extensions. Receivers should use both the RTCP sender report information and the in-band mapping as input to the synchronisation process, and it is recommended that they sanity check the mappings received and discard outliers, to be robust against invalid data of either kind.

Timestamp-based decoding order recovery. Once a receiver has synchronised the components of the flow using the header extensions, it may derive a decoding order from the synchronised timestamps. There may be explicit dependencies between the component flows, for example a hierarchy where flows from higher layers cannot be decoded until the corresponding data in lower layer flows has been received and decoded. If such a decoding hierarchy exists, it must be signalled out of band, for example using RFC 5583 when SDP signalling is used.

Each component RTP flow must contain packets corresponding to all the sampling instants of the RTP flows on which it depends. If such packets are not naturally present, the sender must generate additional packets as necessary. For H.264 SVC, the Empty Network Abstraction Layer unit packet should be used.

The receiver should then decode the packets in all the component flows as follows. For each RTP packet in each flow, use the mapping contained in the header extensions and the sender reports to derive the NTP-format timestamp corresponding to its RTP timestamp. Group together the RTP data packets from all component flows that have identical calculated NTP-format timestamps. Processing groups in order of ascending NTP-format timestamps, decode the RTP packets in each group according to the signalled RTP flow decoding hierarchy, passing the packet data from the flow on which all other flows depend to the decoder first, then that from the next dependent flow, and so on. The decoding order will not necessarily match the packet transmission order, so the receiver needs to buffer packets for a codec-dependent amount of time in order for all necessary packets to arrive.
sections.plainLanguage: When a codec splits the picture across several streams, the receiver has to combine them in the right order before it can decode. The sender stamps each stream at the same sampling instant with the same time value, so the receiver can line them up and then decode in the order the layers depend on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the RTP specification, the extended RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback, and the general mechanism for RTP header extensions apply.

The header extensions defined in Section 3.3 include an NTP-format timestamp. When an RTP session using this header extension is protected by the Secure RTP framework, that header extension is not part of the encrypted portion of the RTP data packets or RTCP control packets, whereas those NTP-format timestamps are encrypted when SRTP is used without this header extension. The RFC calls this a minor information leak that is not believed to be significant. Including the header extension also reduces the efficiency of RTP header compression, and middleboxes that do not understand the header extensions may remove them or may not update the content according to this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: With encrypted RTP, the timestamp carried in the new header extension stays in the clear while the rest of the packet is encrypted. The RFC calls that a small leak and does not think it matters.

The three extensions this RFC defines

items.title: Immediate first report
items.text: A source-specific multicast sender may send its first RTCP packet the moment it joins, because there is only one sender and no risk of a request pile-up.

items.title: Rapid resynchronisation request
items.text: A receiver that is stuck sends a feedback message asking the media source to produce a sender report as soon as possible.

items.title: In-band timestamps
items.text: Two RTP header extensions carry the NTP-format time inside the data packets, so the receiver does not have to infer it from reports.

fields.name: SSRC of packet sender
fields.desc: The member that is unable to synchronise media streams.

fields.desc: The sender of the media that cannot be synchronised.

fields.desc: Length of the extension in 32-bit words minus one.
